html:
A fire that broke out on the night of 18 to 19 July 64 CE among shops by the Circus Maximus and burned for six days, then flared up again for three more. Of Rome's fourteen districts, three were destroyed and seven badly damaged.

The emperor Nero was at Antium on the coast. He came back, opened public buildings and his own gardens to the homeless and brought in grain. But rumours spread that he had started the fire to make room for a new palace, or that he sang of the fall of Troy while the city burned. The tale of him "fiddling" is a later invention; the fiddle did not exist.

To turn the blame, Nero accused the Christians of Rome. Tacitus describes them being torn by dogs and burned as torches. Christian tradition holds that Peter and Paul died in this persecution.

Rome was rebuilt with wider streets, buildings of brick and stone, limits on height and porches in front of houses to fight fires. On a large part of the burned land Nero built his Golden House.
